testCases.input: What is the difference between model evals and application evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
The core distinction is simply what you're pointing the evaluation at. Model evals evaluate the model itself — their job is to test and evaluate LLMs, and the main idea is to test and evaluate the capabilities of a model. Application evals, by contrast, are the evals with which we evaluate LLM-based applications. So one is about the model, and the other is about an application built on top of a model.

To put it in the broader frame: LLM evals are systematic, repeatable tests used to judge an LLM or LLM-powered systems. That definition is why we can say there are two types of LLM evals — model evals and application evals. Model evals are the ones that evaluate the LLM itself, while application evals evaluate LLM-based applications.

It's also worth knowing the purpose behind model evals. The goal is that when a new LLM is released, we test and benchmark its capabilities and document them — which is why you'll see claims that a new LLM came out on top on a particular benchmark or leaderboard, or that it has a certain accuracy or percentage. Model evals can be broken into two kinds: standardized evals, which we call benchmarks (for example, the knowledge-capability benchmarks), and custom model evals, where you make your own dataset and run it to choose a model according to your application.

One important caveat the course emphasizes: the terms "model eval" and "application eval" are not official terms — they were created to simplify the topic. Even now, in the industry, both are just called LLM evals, and people understand from the use case which one is meant. So don't treat them as standard terminology.

Finally, a practical note on why this course focuses on application evals: if you ever watch a video on YouTube titled "LLM evaluation," you can assume it's teaching you application evaluation, not model evaluation — most likely 99% of the time.
